cues.text: On July 25, 1317, a priest from the parish of Viversel , in the Belgian region of Limburg, was called to a gravely ill parishioner’s bedside.
He went to administer the last sacraments; arriving at the house, he set down the bag containing the consecrated Host on a table near the entrance and heard the dying man’s confession.
While the priest was occupied, a curious member of the household opened the bag without being noticed and drew out the pyx.
He touched the Host inside with his hand, then quickly put everything back in order and slipped away, troubled by what he had done.
When the priest returned to give the sick man Communion, he found the Host stained with blood.
Uncertain how to proceed, he sought guidance from the pastor of the neighboring parish of Lumen.
The pastor advised him to carry the Host at once to the Cistercian nuns at the Abbey of Herkenrode .
The Face of Christ Crowned with Thorns
The priest set out for Herkenrode on August 1, 1317, carrying the stained Host in its pyx.

Upon his arrival, he and the assembled community of nuns reported that the Host now showed the image of Christ’s face crowned with thorns, visible upon its surface—a sign attested to, the tradition holds, by numerous witnesses present that day.
The relic remained with the nuns at Herkenrode for nearly five centuries, until the community was expelled during the French Revolution in 1796.
Local families kept the Host hidden through the years of suppression that followed.
It was finally placed for public veneration at the Church of St. Quintinus in Hasselt in 1804, elevated to a cathedral in 1967.

Repeated examinations across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries — including one by an apostolic nuncio and another by the Archbishop of Mechelen — confirmed the relic's continued preservation, and it remains enshrined and venerated in Hasselt to this day.
